Content covers: the school of Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer argument that white garments (worn into the Holy of Holies) should require immersion just as golden garments do, rebutted by the golden garments' broader year-round atonement, with the derivation instead traced to Rebbi's own teaching (l01); Rebbi's own derivation of five immersions and ten sanctifications from 'a sacred linen tunic he shall wear,' with the open question of deriving white-to-golden immersion (l06); the reverse kal vachomer from white to golden garments, with no independent comment on this daf since Rashi's earlier note on l01 already covers the parallel logic (l11); the rebuttal that white garments alone enter the Holy of Holies, resolved by the verse 'they are sacred garments, and he shall bathe his flesh in water and don them' (l14); the mishna's own five-services list, recurring from 32a without new commentary here (l17); the derivation that each immersion requires two sanctifications from the doubled 'and he shall bathe' clause, with Rashi noting the verse could have simply said 'sanctification' directly but chose 'immersion' terminology instead, redirected by the following comment to license deriving actual immersion from this phrase (l20); the further teaching that since immersion is compared to sanctification, both must occur in a sacred place, except the first (non-Torah-level) immersion of the day, which is not derived from this verse (l24); Rabbi Yehuda's alternate derivation of the golden-garment immersion from Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's own reasoning, since he does not read 'they are sacred garments' as teaching sanctification (l27); Rav Chisda's analysis that Rebbi's position diverges from both Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis, requiring two sanctifications bracketing each immersion (once naked, before immersion, and once after dressing) rather than the Rabbis' single dressed-state sanctification, with Rashi's detailed accounting of exactly how Rebbi's reading differs from Rabbi Meir's own mishna-based practice (l28); Rav Acha bar Yaakov's teaching that all authorities, including Rebbi, agree the sanctification immediately preceding a service occurs only once already dressed, derived from the verse's phrase 'or when they approach the altar' (l34); Rav Acha the son of Rava's challenge to Rav Ashi that neither Rav Chisda's nor Rav Acha's own position can be held together without yielding an absurd fifteen sanctifications for Rebbi, with Rashi's arithmetic walking through exactly how three sanctifications per immersion would arise (l38); the mishna's account of the daily-offering's notching and the etymology of 'keratzo' from a root meaning 'slaughter,' cross-referenced to a difficult verse in Nahum and Rav Yosef's own Aramaic rendering, concluding that the notch must be more than half the throat's circumference (l42); Rabbi Yochanan's and Reish Lakish's agreement on the same 'majority of two' standard, with Reish Lakish's own question about why the mishna needed to teach a majority-of-one standard separately for birds when it could be inferred automatically from the general non-sacred-slaughter rule (l47); and the resolution distinguishing a Torah-level invalidation from a merely rabbinic one for an improperly notched daily-offering, since the whole notching requirement exists only to facilitate blood collection (l49). The truncated single-word fragment on the final line ('therefore') is confirmed via modules/yoma/assets/talmuddev/33a.json's first raw Rashi line ('therefore we learned, etc.: from the superfluous teaching, one for non-sacred and one for sacred, since it says...') to be the genuine truncated opening of Rashi's next comment continuing onto 33a, opening an explanation of why the mishna's majority-of-two standard needed restating for consecrated animals; per the established boundary policy it is linked to 32b's own final local segment (l49) rather than invented as a phantom 33a id.
